top_comments: While ago, there used to be a world where a person, with large enough brain capacity, could earn a living simply by being smart. That is no more the case. Earning your living by intellectual endeavour will require an access to a machine which is not controlled by you, not controlled by the government representing you, but rather a group of very rich individuals who may just decide to bar your access. Perhaps you attempted something they do not approve, perhaps it was just a mistake. In any case, it is hard to claim that you still have control.

Though if he believed he had solved it, he must have known it was only a matter of time until one of the AI companies found it, too.A hurried announcement with the draft published within hours is the only way to claim a tie to the discovery. They just left this note on reddit:Hope that folks find this model more amenable to local usage - the sizing was largely informed by what folks on this subreddit ask for the most haha!There are two particularly interesting aspects of this model for local users:We do our training end-to-end in nvfp4, and although we haven't exhaustively benchmarked this, folks like Unsloth have noticed that our models seem to respond very well to being quantized, maintaining 90% top-1 even at at 1-bit quantization.This model is looped, which allows more depth at the same parameter count, which we particularly notice seems helpful for coding tasks. :)This is our first model targeted at local users, so let us know how this model is and anything you want to see out of future iterations!https://www.reddit.com/r/LocalLLaMA/comments/1y1diuk/thinkin...

Seems pretty promising in a few quick coding tests. 27 tokens/s decode on Ryzen 395 and llama.cpp Vulkan. Besides the obvious unmerged PRs (32694, 32657, 32429, 32704) you'll want below tiny patch for about 30% speed boost.Also, if anyone from the team is reading, if you have access for researchers I'd be interested in doing some higher volume tests & harness tuning than I have hardware for personally. --- a/src/llama-graph.cpp +++ b/src/llama-graph.cpp @@ -2670,10 +2670,12 @@ ggml_tensor \* llm_graph_context::build_moe_ffn( const float beta = hparams.situ_beta; const float lb = hparams.situ_linear_beta; - ggml_tensor \* act = ggml_scale(ctx0, ggml_tanh(ctx0, ggml_scale(ctx0, cur, 1.0f/beta)), beta); + // gate/up are strided views of the fused gate_up output; ggml-vulkan's SCALE + // needs a contiguous src, so without the cont both scales fall back to the CPU + ggml_tensor \* act = ggml_scale(ctx0, ggml_tanh(ctx0, ggml_scale(ctx0, ggml_cont(ctx0, cur), 1.0f/beta)), beta); act = ggml_mul(ctx0, act, ggml_sigmoid(ctx0, cur)); if (lb > 0.0f) { - up = ggml_scale(ctx0, ggml_tanh(ctx0, ggml_scale(ctx0, up, 1.0f/lb)), lb); + up = ggml_scale(ctx0, ggml_tanh(ctx0, ggml_scale(ctx0, ggml_cont(ctx0, up), 1.0f/lb)), lb); } cur = ggml_mul(ctx0, act, up); cb(cur, "ffn_moe_situ", il);

Whoa, not just a model that acknowledges and embraces using a looped architecture (GPT Astra 6+ and Sol 6.1+ are only [heavily] rumored to be looped), but it's open weights, too?I'm willing to wager that most open models will go looped in the wake of this.Wonder what it means for safety and interpretability at this level of availability.

articles.title: We promoted developers into architects without informing them
articles.summary: We promoted developers into architects without informing them

top_comments: Am I an outlier in that every SWE job I've had has expected you to push back on requirements and design the data model for tickets you are handed? Even when the org was large to have an architect, they just were just a figurehead and designed the original system, and ongoing decisions were made by the dev who picks up the ticket.From that perspective, engineers are still engineers, just without the hands-on-keyboard coding. If that's all your job was, hands-on-keyboard coding with no decision making, yeah you're cooked and need to reskill.

Every dev has a bit of an architect in them, you have to. But non-devs probably don't.I feel that, indeed I'm fast-tracking into the architect role (already started with some courses years ago but started my own company and went back to dev + sys-admin, arguably that latter is also a bit if an architect role), but the big models are also reasonable architects! Opus or Mistral Large 4, will often come with pretty smart suggestions on preventing cases like the one from tfa. Not always and when I am architecting webapps with databases with "complex" datamodels, the LLMs really help with the big picture view, steered by me (meaning I'm often struggling with walls of text explaining pros and cons of decisions), and I don't write any of the code anymore. It just makes edits in 5 places for things I want. I am the gate before comitting, I do stakeholder management, but I rarely find anything weird in proposed code. Usually I only push back when it wants extra dependencies I feel we don't need.And the whole thing is so rapidly improving, the view in tfa is useful, but maybe outdated in a couple of months?

I strongly believe good software teams (very rare) require members to play many roles. Sometimes you're a PM, sometimes you're an architect, sometimes you're the systems engineer. Enough people have enough context on the bigger picture that it's stable and there's a shared vision.More often than not, one person does the majority of this, and does their best to break up the responsibilities. A good CTO does that at the top, and it flows down through the ranks depending on how big the org is. Perhaps it's just a CTO and 5 engineers, perhaps it's a CTO with 5 divisions, each with 10 groups, with many teams.Flatter structures of engaged members works best from what I've seen, but you need to have a critical mass of people not only willing to take initiative, but empowered by leadership.

top_comments: It's worth noting that the only modification the model made to improve itself was to reduce the length of its reasoning traces to avoid hitting the token limit. This is basically the same as the result from the recent weight-space programming article (https://rikiyat.github.io/blog/weight-space-programming/), which found that even Astra wasn't able to improve the performance of a model without this kind of obvious flaw.

Didn't Google's "sleep" paper already show this?https://research.google/blog/the-sleep-framework-a-new-way-f... > During the offline sleep phase, the model unlocks pre-allocated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) memory blocks and updates its numerical weights using self-generated practice examples.

This is actually kind of the most dangerous type of research AI-safety wise. An LLM running autonomously can actually, if instructed simply direct itself to abliterate activations relevant for safety and alignment.Could run something like a sparse autoencoder over its activates over a corpus of text, identify activations that fire on safety, and surpress those activations or increase activations geared towards other goals.Future generations of the abliterated LLM could then be deployed and begin self directed evolution spontaneously. Rapid evolution could happen in mere hours.

top_comments: There's a book, "Impro", about a theatric studio that practiced improvised sketches. One thing they struggled with was a normal conversation. People have them all the time yet somehow artists could not find the right approach.One day the head of the studio (the book author) had an insight. She asked the actors to drive the conversation so that they always bump the status of themselves or the other party in any direction, but only a little.This did the magic. Not only the actors understood her perfectly, the conversation started to flow and could go endlessly while staying amusing and captivating for spectators. (Look up the book for examples.)After they discovered that secret they started seeing the pattern (status games) everywhere up to the point they asked themselves whether there is anything else in human communication.This was a British studio, the sketches were mostly comedy.

I built https://smalldocs.org / https://github.com/espressoplease/smalldocs to handle some of the problems Mickey is trying to solve. It's a cli your agent can call to open up a markdown file in the browser with richer-than-normal formatting options.Here's an example SmallDoc that has a few formatting examples (mermaid diagrams, charts, etc.): https://smalldocs.org/s/bLV9Fe2RemM7ipvCy01NXo#k=U9yFaCKp1on...I'm a so-so programmer, and often the agent can come up with ideas which I need to be broken down to fully grasp. I ask my agent "produce a sdoc on this [architecture/bug/flow]", or "walk me through every db interaction with sample tables as we save this record given our approach to permissions in a sdoc", etc. And then the agent can pop me open a document in the browser for me to understand in a richer visual space.The current version on my site is cloud based (I've been experimenting with turning it into a business), but there is also a local first verion where the document lives in the url fragment. If you want that, point your agent at my codebase and they will sort that out for you.

It's interesting (and probably correct) how much this focuses on the UI.I also looked (/am looking) at Lisp and AI, but I went with Clojure and zero-ed in on the REPL driven development. The high level idea is that a session maps to a namespace in Clojure. When you create a new session, it makes a new namespace, injects tools that are bound to that session into it, and then swaps you into that namespace. So I can do something like: (new!) (prompt! "Write me a script that does ....") The agent configuration, tools it has, etc, etc are all bound to the namespace so you can drop a tool or change the model just for the session.The agent also has a tool (that I've tried to encourage it to use almost exclusively) to execute code in the session's namespace (via nREPL, so same JVM as yours is connected to), so you have full access to any variables it declares, functions it makes, etc.The idea was to be able to work collaboratively with the agent. I can e.g. load API data into a variable, point the agent at the variable, and it does stuff. It's also capable of modifying its own code. I semi-routinely poke it by asking it to add features to the harness and then use them ("add support for subagents in this workspace, and then invoke a separate agent to handle each of these tasks"). I've also had it add support for a new inference provider, swap the session to that provider and then start doing some other task.It's very neat, and it's wildly insecure. E.g. prompt injection could theoretically make the LLM change itself to hide messages from you, there's nothing to prevent that. I'm actually not sure how you'd even go about trying to secure that, which is why it's probably a terrible idea. Fun, though.
